title: Strangers everywhere (Diognetus 5)
hook: Christians marry, eat and live like others, yet live as citizens of heaven
tomorrow: why would a vision show the church as an old woman growing young?

segments.voice: In a roaring stadium, Polycarp spoke of a lifetime's friendship and gave thanks before the fire. Eighty-six years. Now a letter about ordinary Christians on ordinary streets.

Scroll a stranger's profile and you can usually guess a few things: the team, the music, the city. A man named Diognetus wanted to size up the Christians that way. Who is this God they trust? Why do they love one another? Someone wrote him an answer, a short letter that never gives its writer's name. And in chapter five, instead of a list of beliefs, the writer describes how Christians actually live. It starts with a surprise: you can't pick them out of a crowd.
screen: `SIZING UP A STRANGER.` → `DIOGNETUS ASKS.` → `YOU CAN'T PICK THEM OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the picture, in plain words. Christians aren't set apart by country, or language, or customs. They don't live in cities of their own. They live in whatever city their lot falls in, and follow the local ways in clothing and food and the rest of ordinary life. They marry like everyone. They have children, and they don't abandon them. They share their table with others, but not their bed. So far, nothing to see. Then the sentences start folding back on themselves. They live in their own countries, but as visitors. Every foreign land is home to them, and every home is a foreign land. They spend their days on earth, but they are citizens of heaven. They obey the laws, and their lives go further than the laws ask. Paul says something close to the Philippians: "For our conversation is in heaven," conversation meaning the whole way a person lives. So the difference isn't walls or costumes. It's where the deepest belonging lies, and it shows in small things: a table shared, a child kept, a law kept and then some.
screen: `SAME CITIES, SAME FOOD.` · `EVERY FOREIGN LAND IS HOME.` · `ON EARTH, CITIZENS OF HEAVEN.` · `DIFFERENT WITHIN, NOT WALLED OFF.` · then, large: `CITIZENS OF HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Take one ordinary message you'd send today anyway, to a friend, a coworker, a parent, and write it now, a little warmer or more honest than you usually would. Send it if it feels right, and let the rest of the sit be quiet.
Strangers everywhere. The Letter to Diognetus on how Christians live: at home in every city, and visitors in all of them.
Your line: citizens of heaven. Same streets, same food, a different home. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians read the Letter to Diognetus as an early picture of living among neighbors, and some churches read chapter five aloud as a reminder of ordinary faithfulness.

chat.meaning: The Letter to Diognetus says Christians live in ordinary cities by ordinary customs, yet belong to heaven. Same outside, different within: not hidden, not a costume.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (life shape: what do you change, and what do you keep, in a new place?). Title, word, carry and sources kept; Philippians 3:20 added.

Diognetus 5 is paraphrased throughout (Lightfoot 1891 is public domain, but the writer was not certain of its exact wording). Confirm the paraphrase: 'they don't abandon them' renders the line about not casting away offspring; 'love everyone' and 'treated badly by many' were cut for length.
'A short letter that never gives its writer's name': the text names no author; confirm this framing.
Philippians 3:20 'conversation' glossed as 'the whole way a person lives' (as on day 1589 for Hebrews 13:7); the trapdoor names it a citizen's word (Greek πολίτευμα). Standard lexicon; confirm.
Unity note: the letter's picture of Christians sharing ordinary life with every city's people ('every foreign land is home') is kept as the lesson's center; no other tradition is described.
Original: πολιτεύονται (Diognetus 5.9, 'ἐν οὐρανῷ πολιτεύονται'); confirm spelling and pronunciation.
Grace storyline, day 12: Pop cried at her news, then said 'go', adding 'stay the same girl out there'; Grace wonders if she should hide her faith at the program. Practice kind: text someone.
